plan: SAT R&W batch 72: 20 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000644..000663, weighted toward Standard English Conventions (9 SEC: Rudolph boundary, Bayeux paired dashes, pistol shrimp colon, Mesa Verde plural possessive, Dead Sea Scrolls agreement, Merian pronoun, Cannon past perfect, Ibn Battuta modifier, Alice Ball finite verb), plus Potter negation WIC, ozone WIC, Rubin purpose, Talas/Bloom cross-text, Payne inference, Meitner central idea, coral moonlight evidence, commute data, E. E. Just and Nok transitions, and Leavitt synthesis. Topics checked against both workstreams (Claude banks/drafts and ChatGPT baseline text). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: From brace to finish line
passages.text: As a child, Wilma Rudolph wore a brace on her left leg after a bout of ______ by 1960, she had become one of the fastest runners in the world, winning three gold medals in track and field at the Olympic Games in Rome.

passages.title: Not quite a tapestry
passages.text: The Bayeux Tapestry — which, despite its name, is an embroidery stitched in wool on linen rather than a woven ______ depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England in 1066.

passages.title: A shrimp with a sound
passages.text: The pistol shrimp hunts with sound rather than with a ______ its oversized claw shut so quickly that it creates a bubble whose collapse produces a loud crack, which stuns nearby prey.

passages.title: Homes in the cliffs
passages.text: Between about 1190 and 1280, the ______ multistory homes were built into large alcoves in the cliffs of Mesa Verde, in what is now southwestern Colorado. Some, like the structure now called Cliff Palace, contained more than one hundred rooms.

passages.title: Scrolls in the caves
passages.text: In 1947, Bedouin shepherds found ancient scrolls stored in clay jars in caves near Qumran, close to the Dead Sea. Over the following decade, researchers recovered fragments of roughly 900 manuscripts from nearby caves. Some of the scrolls, which were written between about the third century BCE and the first century CE, ______ the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible.

passages.title: Life cycles on the page
passages.text: In 1699, the German-born artist and naturalist Maria Sibylla Merian sailed to Suriname to study insects in their habitats. In her book Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium (1705), each of the sixty plates shows an insect at several stages of ______ life, together with the plant on which it feeds.

passages.title: Three hundred fifty thousand stars
passages.text: At the Harvard College Observatory, Annie Jump Cannon could classify a star by its spectrum in seconds. By the time she retired in 1940, she ______ roughly 350,000 stars, more than any other astronomer, using a system of letters (O, B, A, F, G, K, M) that astronomers still use.

passages.title: Thirty years on the road
passages.text: Ibn Battuta became one of the most widely traveled people of the medieval world. Setting out from his home city of Tangier in 1325 at the age of twenty-one, ______

passages.title: A chemist's method
passages.text: In 1915, Alice Ball, a twenty-three-year-old chemist at the College of Hawaii, ______ a method for turning oil from the seeds of the chaulmoogra tree into a form that could be injected to treat leprosy. She died the following year, and for decades her contribution went largely unrecognized.

passages.title: Spores and watercolors
passages.text: Beatrix Potter had no university training in science, but she was hardly a ______ observer of fungi. She produced hundreds of precise watercolors of mushrooms and wrote a paper on how their spores germinate, which was presented on her behalf to the Linnean Society of London in 1897, since women were not then permitted to attend its meetings.

passages.title: A hole in the sky
passages.text: In 1985, scientists of the British Antarctic Survey reported a ______ decline in the ozone above Antarctica each spring: measured levels had fallen far below anything recorded at their station in earlier decades. The finding helped prompt the 1987 Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to phase out chemicals that destroy ozone.

passages.title: Galaxies that spin too fast
passages.text: In the 1970s, astronomer Vera Rubin and her colleague Kent Ford measured how fast stars orbit the centers of spiral galaxies. If most of a galaxy's mass were in its bright central region, stars far from the center should orbit more slowly. Instead, Rubin found that outer stars moved about as fast as inner ones. The simplest explanation was that galaxies contain large amounts of unseen matter, which astronomers now call dark matter.

passages.title: How paper traveled west
passages.text:
Text 1
According to a story repeated in many histories, Chinese papermakers captured at the Battle of Talas in 751 taught their craft to their captors, and papermaking spread from Samarkand to Baghdad and the rest of the Islamic world as a result.

Text 2
Historian Jonathan Bloom notes that this story first appears in sources written centuries after the battle. He also points out that paper was already being used in Central Asia well before 751, which suggests that knowledge of papermaking had reached the region by other routes.

passages.title: Mostly hydrogen
passages.text: In the 1920s, most astronomers assumed that stars were made of roughly the same mix of elements as Earth. In her 1925 doctoral thesis, Cecilia Payne used the spectra of stars to conclude that they are composed overwhelmingly of hydrogen and helium. The astronomer Henry Norris Russell, an influential expert, persuaded her to describe this result as "almost certainly not real." In 1929, Russell reached the same conclusion by other methods, and Payne's finding is now accepted. Based on the text, Russell's initial objection most likely reflected ______

passages.title: Splitting the nucleus
passages.text: In December 1938, chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin reported that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced barium, a much lighter element, but they could not explain how. Lise Meitner, who had worked with Hahn for decades before fleeing Nazi Germany earlier that year, discussed the result with her nephew, physicist Otto Frisch. Together they proposed that the uranium nucleus had split in two, calculated the enormous energy released, and named the process fission. In 1944, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery was awarded to Hahn alone.

passages.title: Spawning by moonlight
passages.text: On the Great Barrier Reef, many coral colonies release their eggs and sperm on just a few nights each year, usually several nights after a full moon in late spring. Some researchers hypothesize that moonlight is one of the cues that tells corals when to spawn.

passages.title: Getting to school
passages.text:
A student surveyed 120 classmates about how they usually travel to school.
Bus: 48 students
Walk: 30 students
Car: 24 students
Bike: 18 students
The student claims that walking and biking together were exactly as common as taking the bus.

passages.title: A scientist abroad
passages.text: Ernest Everett Just, a biologist at Howard University, published widely respected research on fertilization and the cell surface in marine animals. Yet because of racial discrimination, he was never offered a position at the predominantly white research universities of his day. ______ he spent much of the 1930s working in European laboratories, including the zoological station in Naples, Italy, where he found the research conditions he had been denied at home.

passages.title: Lost layers
passages.text: The Nok culture of what is now central Nigeria is known for its terracotta sculptures, some of them more than 2,000 years old. Many of these figures were discovered in the twentieth century by tin miners digging in the region. ______ because most were removed from the ground without careful recording, archaeologists often cannot tell exactly where, or in what layer of soil, a particular figure was found.

passages.title: Notes on a variable star
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Henrietta Swan Leavitt worked at the Harvard College Observatory in the early 1900s.
- She studied Cepheid variable stars, which brighten and dim on a regular cycle.
- In 1912, she reported that brighter Cepheids have longer cycles.
- Because of this relationship, a Cepheid's cycle reveals its true brightness, and comparing true brightness with how bright it appears reveals its distance.
- In the 1920s, Edwin Hubble used Cepheids to show that some galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: she had become one of the fastest runners in the world
candidates.explanation: Both parts are independent clauses, so a semicolon correctly separates them.

A.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

C.rationale: "Then" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so the comma still joins two independent clauses.

D.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

hints: Can both parts stand alone as sentences?

strategy.explanation: Find where the first clause ends.

candidates.remember: Join independent clauses with a semicolon or a period, not a comma alone.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest
candidates.explanation: The supplementary clause opened with a dash must be closed with a matching dash before the verb "depicts."

A.rationale: A dash opens the supplement, so a dash, not a comma, must close it.

B.rationale: A semicolon cannot separate the subject from its verb "depicts."

C.rationale: Without closing punctuation, the supplement runs into the main verb.

hints: How does the interrupting clause begin?

strategy.explanation: Match the punctuation that opens the supplement.

candidates.remember: Close a supplement with the same mark that opened it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: its oversized claw shut so quickly
candidates.explanation: A colon after the complete clause correctly introduces the phrase that explains how the shrimp hunts with sound.

B.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "snapping its oversized claw..." is a phrase.

C.rationale: "Snapping its oversized claw shut..." has no main verb, so it would be a fragment.

D.rationale: "And" joins the participial phrase as if it were a second verb, which is ungrammatical here.

hints: Is what follows a complete sentence or an explanation?

strategy.explanation: Check what each side of the blank needs.

candidates.remember: A colon can introduce an explanation after a complete clause.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: multistory homes were built into large alcoves
candidates.explanation: The homes belonged to many people, so the plural possessive "Ancestral Puebloans'" is correct.

A.rationale: This singular possessive refers to one person, but many people built the homes.

B.rationale: The homes belong to the people, so a possessive form is needed.

D.rationale: A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe.

hints: How many people does the noun name, and do they own something?

strategy.explanation: Decide plural or singular, then possessive.

candidates.remember: Plural possessive: add an apostrophe after the s.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Some of the scrolls, which were written between about the third century BCE
candidates.explanation: "Some of the scrolls" is plural, so it takes the plural verb "are"; the intervening clause does not change the subject.

A.rationale: "Some of the scrolls" refers to more than one scroll, so the verb must be plural.

B.rationale: The singular verb does not agree with the plural subject "Some of the scrolls."

C.rationale: "Being" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

hints: Does "Some" refer to one scroll or several here?

strategy.explanation: Cross out the nonessential clause between the commas.

candidates.remember: "Some" takes a plural verb when it refers to a plural noun.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: shows an insect at several stages of
candidates.explanation: The pronoun refers to "an insect," which is singular, so the possessive "its" is correct.

A.rationale: "Their" is plural, but it refers to the singular "an insect."

C.rationale: "It's" means "it is," which makes no sense here.

D.rationale: "His or her" refers to people, but the antecedent is an insect.

hints: Whose life does each plate show?

strategy.explanation: Find the pronoun's antecedent.

candidates.remember: A singular antecedent takes a singular pronoun.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: By the time she retired in 1940
candidates.explanation: "By the time she retired in 1940" marks a past point, and the classifying was complete before it, so the past perfect "had classified" is needed.

A.rationale: The present perfect does not fit an action completed before a past point (her retirement in 1940).

B.rationale: The present tense does not fit events that ended in 1940.

D.rationale: "Would classify" suggests a future action, but the classifying was already complete by 1940.

hints: Was the classifying finished before or after 1940?

strategy.explanation: Look for a time marker that sets a past reference point.

candidates.remember: Use the past perfect for an action completed before another past time.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Ibn Battuta traveled for nearly thirty years through North Africa, the Middle East, and Asia.
choices.B: nearly thirty years of travel took Ibn Battuta through North Africa, the Middle East, and Asia.
choices.C: the journeys of Ibn Battuta lasted nearly thirty years through North Africa, the Middle East, and Asia.
choices.D: North Africa, the Middle East, and Asia were all visited by Ibn Battuta over nearly thirty years.

candidates.evidence: Setting out from his home city of Tangier in 1325
candidates.explanation: The opening phrase describes Ibn Battuta, so his name must come immediately after the comma.

B.rationale: The years of travel did not set out from Tangier; the modifier must be followed by Ibn Battuta.

C.rationale: The journeys did not set out at age twenty-one; Ibn Battuta did.

D.rationale: The regions did not set out from Tangier; the modifier dangles.

hints: Who set out from Tangier?

strategy.explanation: Find the noun the opening phrase describes.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier must be followed by the noun it describes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: a method for turning oil from the seeds of the chaulmoogra tree
candidates.explanation: The subject "Alice Ball" needs a main verb; "developed" supplies it, and the appositive between commas does not.

A.rationale: "Developing" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

B.rationale: "Who developed" turns the predicate into a clause, leaving the sentence without a main verb.

C.rationale: "Having developed" is a participle, so the sentence would lack a main verb.

hints: What is the main verb of the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence without the appositive.

candidates.remember: Every sentence needs a finite main verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: She produced hundreds of precise watercolors of mushrooms
candidates.explanation: "Hardly" negates the word that follows, and the evidence shows serious, careful work, so she was hardly a "casual" observer.

A.rationale: "Hardly a careful observer" would mean she was careless, which contradicts her precise work.

C.rationale: "Hardly a dedicated observer" contradicts the hundreds of paintings and the paper.

D.rationale: "Hardly a skilled observer" contradicts the description of her precise watercolors.

hints: What does "hardly" do to the word that follows it?

strategy.explanation: Predict a word meaning "not serious" that "hardly" can deny.

candidates.remember: Watch for negating words such as "hardly" that reverse a blank's meaning.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: had fallen far below anything recorded at their station in earlier decades
candidates.explanation: Levels falling "far below anything recorded" indicate a steep, dramatic drop, so "precipitous" fits.

A.rationale: A decline "far below anything recorded" is large, not negligible.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests the decline was expected; it was a surprising finding.

D.rationale: The text gives no evidence that the decline was brief.

hints: How large was the decline?

strategy.explanation: Predict "steep" from the text after the colon.

candidates.remember: Use the explanation after the colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that the bright central regions of galaxies contain most of the mass in those galaxies
choices.B: To explain how astronomers measure the distances between neighboring galaxies
choices.C: To compare the careers of two astronomers who studied spiral galaxies
choices.D: To describe an unexpected measurement and the explanation that astronomers accepted

candidates.evidence: Instead, Rubin found that outer stars moved about as fast as inner ones
candidates.explanation: The text states an expectation, reports a measurement that contradicted it, and gives the explanation, unseen matter, that followed.

A.rationale: The text says the measurements contradicted this expectation.

B.rationale: The text concerns orbital speeds within galaxies, not distances between them.

C.rationale: Ford is mentioned only as Rubin's colleague; careers are not compared.

hints: What does "Instead" signal?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence's role.

candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Bloom (Text 2) most likely respond to the story described in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the evidence makes the story an unlikely explanation for how papermaking spread
choices.B: By agreeing that the Battle of Talas introduced paper to Central Asia but disputing its date
choices.C: By claiming that papermaking spread from Baghdad eastward to China rather than westward
choices.D: By proving that no Chinese papermakers were ever captured at the Battle of Talas

candidates.evidence: paper was already being used in Central Asia well before 751
candidates.explanation: Bloom notes that the story appears only in much later sources and that paper was in use in Central Asia before the battle, so he would doubt that the battle explains the spread.

B.rationale: Bloom says paper was used in Central Asia before 751, so he would not agree that the battle introduced it.

C.rationale: Text 2 says nothing about paper moving from Baghdad to China.

D.rationale: Bloom questions the story's sources; he does not prove that no one was captured.

hints: What two points does Bloom make?

strategy.explanation: Compare each point with the story in Text 1.

candidates.remember: A cross-text response can question both a source and its conclusion.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a mistake in the spectra that Payne had collected for her thesis.
choices.B: Russell's own earlier measurements showing that stars contain little hydrogen.
choices.C: the widely held view that stars resembled Earth in composition.
choices.D: a general rule that doctoral theses should not include new conclusions.

candidates.evidence: most astronomers assumed that stars were made of roughly the same mix of elements as Earth
candidates.explanation: Payne's result contradicted the common assumption that stars resembled Earth, which best explains why Russell doubted it before reaching the same conclusion himself.

A.rationale: The text gives no indication that her spectra were flawed; her result was later confirmed.

B.rationale: The text does not mention any earlier measurements by Russell.

D.rationale: Nothing in the text suggests such a rule.

hints: What did most astronomers believe at the time?

strategy.explanation: Connect the objection to the belief stated in the first sentence.

candidates.remember: Look for the earlier sentence that explains a later reaction.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Hahn and Strassmann discovered fission and correctly explained it without any help from other scientists.
choices.B: Meitner helped explain a key discovery in nuclear physics but was left out of the prize that honored it.
choices.C: Meitner left Germany because she disagreed with Hahn about how to interpret their experiments.
choices.D: Frisch named the process of fission only after calculating how much energy the splitting uranium released.

candidates.evidence: Together they proposed that the uranium nucleus had split in two
candidates.explanation: The text shows that Meitner and Frisch explained the Berlin result as fission, yet only Hahn received the Nobel Prize.

A.rationale: The text says they could not explain their result; Meitner and Frisch did.

C.rationale: The text says she fled Nazi Germany, not that she left over a scientific disagreement.

D.rationale: This is one detail, and the text credits Meitner and Frisch together.

hints: What is the text mainly about, and how does it end?

strategy.explanation: Combine the explanation and the final sentence.

candidates.remember: A main idea covers the whole text, not one detail.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (finding that supports a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.A: Coral colonies in warmer parts of the reef spawned slightly earlier in the year than colonies in cooler parts.
choices.B: Many species of fish gather near reefs to feed on coral eggs on the nights when spawning occurs.
choices.C: Coral colonies that spawn on the same nights often belong to several different species living near one another.
choices.D: Corals in tanks spawned on a schedule matching an artificial moon cycle rather than the real one.

candidates.evidence: moonlight is one of the cues that tells corals when to spawn
candidates.explanation: If changing the light cycle shifts the spawning schedule, moonlight is directly shown to act as a cue.

A.rationale: This links spawning to temperature, not to moonlight.

B.rationale: This describes what happens during spawning, not what triggers it.

C.rationale: This shows spawning is shared across species but does not identify moonlight as a cue.

hints: What kind of finding would isolate moonlight as the cause?

strategy.explanation: Look for a result that changes when only the light changes.

candidates.remember: The strongest support tests the specific cause the hypothesis names.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Thirty students walked and 18 biked, a combined 48, the same number as took the bus.
choices.B: Forty-eight students took the bus, more than used any other single way of getting to school.
choices.C: Thirty students walked to school, which was more than the 18 students who biked there.
choices.D: Twenty-four students came by car, which was exactly half the number who took the bus.

candidates.evidence: walking and biking together were exactly as common as taking the bus
candidates.explanation: The claim combines walking and biking: 30 + 18 = 48, which equals the 48 bus riders. Only this choice makes that comparison.

B.rationale: This is true but says nothing about walking and biking combined.

C.rationale: This compares walking with biking rather than combining them.

D.rationale: This compares car with bus, which is not the claim.

hints: Which two numbers does the claim combine?

strategy.explanation: Add the categories the claim groups together.

candidates.remember: Match the data to the exact comparison the claim makes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: where he found the research conditions he had been denied at home
candidates.explanation: Being shut out of research positions at home led Just to work in Europe, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.

A.rationale: Working abroad does not contrast with being denied positions at home; it follows from it.

B.rationale: Working in Europe is not similar to being denied positions; it is a result.

D.rationale: Working in Europe is not an example of discrimination; it is a response to it.

hints: Is working in Europe a result of the previous sentence or a contrast with it?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Use "Consequently" when one event results from another.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: archaeologists often cannot tell exactly where
candidates.explanation: The final sentence describes a regrettable result of how the figures were found, so "Unfortunately" fits.

A.rationale: The lost information is not similar to the discovery by miners; it is a regrettable consequence.

C.rationale: The final sentence does not restate the previous one.

D.rationale: The final sentence is not an example of the miners' discoveries.

hints: Is the final sentence good news or bad news for archaeologists?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Choose a transition that matches the writer's attitude and logic.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain the significance of Leavitt's discovery to an audience unfamiliar with Cepheid stars. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, who worked at the Harvard College Observatory in the early 1900s, studied Cepheid variable stars, which brighten and dim on a regular, repeating cycle.
choices.B: In 1912, Henrietta Swan Leavitt reported that the brighter Cepheid variable stars in her study at the Harvard College Observatory had longer cycles than the dimmer ones did.
choices.C: Leavitt found that a Cepheid's cycle reveals its true brightness, letting astronomers measure distances, as Hubble did to show other galaxies lie far beyond ours.
choices.D: In the 1920s, the astronomer Edwin Hubble used Cepheid variable stars, which brighten and dim on a regular cycle, to show that some galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way.

candidates.evidence: a Cepheid's cycle reveals its true brightness
candidates.explanation: Only this choice explains what the discovery made possible, measuring distances, and how it was later used.

A.rationale: This describes what Leavitt studied but not why her discovery mattered.

B.rationale: This states the finding but does not explain its significance to an unfamiliar audience.

D.rationale: This describes Hubble's work without connecting it to Leavitt's discovery.

hints: Which choice says why the discovery mattered?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must accomplish the stated goal.
